findings.matters: Staff retention and recruitment pressure during reorganisation can affect service delivery and costs for councils going through LGR, and their peers may be facing the same.
findings.figures: score 9 (likelihood 3 × impact 3); acceptable score 8

findings.headline: The corporate risk on legal cases against the Council is to be de-escalated, with a score of 6 against an acceptable score of 10.
findings.detail: The register lists the likelihood at 2 and the impact at 3 and states the risk is to be de-escalated. Actions include identifying where service failure lies in a legal case and reviewing the existing service level agreement with the Monitoring Officer.
findings.matters: A downgrade in a legal risk is a governance decision that peers and auditors may compare with their own registers.

findings.headline: The temporary accommodation risk impact has been reduced from catastrophic to major, with the score at 16 against an acceptable score of 8
findings.detail: The register says the risk is now categorised as financial, although it concerns housing. It also states that many of its causes are outside the local authority's control and cannot be mitigated successfully. Mitigations include the expanded Rother Tenant Finder and continued investment in the council's own temporary accommodation stock.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are a demand-led pressure many councils face, and a reduced impact rating reflects how the council has re-assessed its exposure.
findings.figures: score 16 (likelihood 4 × impact 4); acceptable score 8
findings.quote: The impact has been reduced from catastrophic to major.

findings.headline: Project delivery and budget risk is scored 12 against an acceptable score of 8, with its likelihood score increased due to likely increased costs across a number of major schemes.
findings.detail: The register says mitigation plans are in place but overspend is likely unless further external funding can be accessed. It notes the Capital Development Programme and Fit for the Future Programme are being reviewed in light of local government reorganisation (LGR).
findings.matters: A council that expects major capital schemes to overspend without extra grant is a concern for its own finance team and for lenders assessing its capital programme.
findings.figures: score 12 (likelihood 3 × impact 4); acceptable score 8
findings.quote: Mitigation plans are in place but overspend is likely unless further external funding can be accessed.

findings.headline: Corporate budget and reserves risk is scored 25 against an acceptable 8, with 'Consider Exceptional Financial Support' among further actions
findings.detail: The register says the score reflects 'the ongoing financial pressures the Council is under particularly due to the cost of living'. Further actions include 'Consider Exceptional Financial Support', 'Review Earmarked Reserves' and 'Review savings plans to see where more savings can be made'. Monthly monitoring of the savings plan is led by the S151 officer.
findings.matters: A council listing Exceptional Financial Support as a further action, with reserves under review, is a signal finance directors and lenders watch closely.
findings.figures: score 25 (likelihood 5 × impact 5); acceptable score 8
findings.quote: This score reflects the ongoing financial pressures the Council is under particularly due to the cost of living.

findings.headline: Final disposal of open market sale homes at the Blackfriars scheme is now expected by 31/05/29, 14 months after the original forecast.
findings.detail: The register says the first phase of homes has been released and two open market sales have been agreed and await completion. It attributes the delay partly to the Middle East conflict and forecast rises in bank and mortgage rates. It states that the risk should diminish as homes are completed and sold, if the revised sales schedule is achieved.
findings.matters: Slippage in disposal dates on a council-backed development affects when loans are repaid and is relevant to any council running a similar housing vehicle.
findings.figures: 14 months later than originally forecast; 31/05/29 final disposal date; 2 open market sales agreed; 70 OMS units
findings.quote: Final disposal of OMS homes is not now expected until 31/05/29

findings.headline: A Rother District Council Housing Company and Blackfriars development risk carries a potential maximum loan exposure of £40m to the Council and is scored 25 against an acceptable score of 8.
findings.detail: The risk covers the ability to sell 70 open market sale units at the values assumed and the housing company's ability to repay loans to the Council. The register says the scheme 'carries the highest level of risk to the Council'. Mitigations include 130 units pre-sold to Places for People (PfP).
findings.matters: A finance director, here or elsewhere, would want to know the size of the council's loan exposure to a housing company and the sales assumptions behind its repayment.

findings.headline: Rother's Q2 forecast closing capital financing requirement for 2026/27 is £90.8m, against £82.2m in the original budget

findings.figures: Revised budget £4,486,550; forecast £4,038,376; variance -£448,174

findings.detail: The Planning, Coastal & Emergency Management line is forecast to overspend by £314,597 at P5. The paper's table does not state the cause.

findings.headline: The auditor raised seven recommendations, one high-priority on publishing the signed Annual Governance Statement and six medium-priority.
findings.detail: The high-priority item is that the draft signed Annual Governance Statement on the council's website does not show approval and signatures. Management accepts the recommendation and says the signed copy will be uploaded. findings.matters: A finance director at another council would compare the number and type of recommendations against their own audit, and the AGS publication point is a governance requirement.

findings.headline: The audit moved £3,510,822 of Community Infrastructure Levy debtors from short-term to long-term and restated the 2024/25 comparative balance sheet by £1,477,625.
findings.detail: The misclassification was material to the prior-year comparatives, so the 2024/25 balance sheet has been amended. The overall effect on the 2025/26 comprehensive income statement and general fund is nil.
findings.matters: A restated prior-year comparative is a visible change to the balance sheet that a reader comparing councils' year-on-year figures will need to understand.
findings.figures: £3,510,822 CIL reclassified from short-term to long-term debtors; £1,477,625 2024/25 comparative amendment
findings.quote: During the current year audit, we identified a material misclassification between short-term and long-term debtors relating to Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) balances.

findings.headline: Brought-forward short-term creditors of £151k, outstanding for more than a year, have had £50k resolved, and the auditor has left the recommendation open for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The other prior-year items still open are an uncleared reconciling balance in the Benefits Lloyds bank account, which has been unresolved for over 12 months, and the absence of a signed shared legal services agreement with Wealden District Council. The auditor says the Wealden agreement remains outstanding.
findings.matters: Aged creditors and unreconciled bank balances are balance sheet hygiene points that auditors track year to year, and a finance director would want to see them cleared.
findings.figures: £151k brought-forward creditors; £50k resolved; reconciling items uncleared for over 12 months
findings.quote: The Council is continuing to resolve this, having resolved £50k of the brought forward balance and continues to work through the remaining.

findings.headline: A control weakness from the 2024/25 audit, where system administrators could also post journals, is marked as completed after a trainee accountant took over journal posting in January 2026.
findings.detail: The auditor says the council had not implemented the change for 2025/26, so it was taken into account in the risk assessment, and testing found no issues. The auditor's follow-up table marks the action as completed.
findings.matters: Segregation of duties over journals is a core control, and other councils with the same system setup will want to see how Rother closed the point.
findings.figures: New trainee accountant employed January 2026
findings.quote: The Council employed a new trainee accountant in January 2026 who is responsible for posting journals and taking over the responsibility from the system administrators.

findings.headline: The auditor identified no significant weaknesses in Rother's value-for-money arrangements and made two recommendations on financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The two recommendations cover savings plans, which should rest on realistic, deliverable assumptions with clear implementation plans, and governance of lending to Rother Housing Company. The lending recommendation asks for formalised lending arrangements and better monitoring of the company's financial performance, development delivery, and ability to repay.
findings.matters: Savings deliverability and lending governance to a council-owned company are the two financial sustainability issues other councils and lenders would compare against their own positions.
findings.figures: Two financial sustainability improvement recommendations
findings.quote: We identified no significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements.

findings.headline: The council's loan to Rother Housing Company, £9.7m including interest at 31 March 2025, had received no repayment of capital or interest, and the company reported losses in the two years to March 2025.
findings.detail: The auditor's expected credit loss estimate was prepared by an external expert, Arling Close, and the auditor found no issues with it. The critical judgement note understated the approved loan facility, which should be £40m. Management says the loan agreement with the company was signed in July 2025.
findings.matters: A council lending to its own company, with no repayment and recurring losses, is the exposure a lender or finance director would most want to see quantified.
findings.figures: £9.7m loan and interest at 31 March 2025; £40m approved loan facility; losses in the last two financial years to March 2025
findings.quote: To date, the Council has received no repayment of the capital and interest and we note the Company has reported a loss in the last two financial years to March 2025.

findings.headline: Auditor testing found property valuations overstated by £933,000 for land and buildings and £360,000 for investment property, because floor areas and rent data held by the council differed from those given to the valuer.
findings.detail: Floor area discrepancies in four sampled land and buildings properties produced the £933,000 overstatement. One investment property had floor area errors and two had inaccurate rental income, and a £581,000 asset was classified as investment property. It has been reclassified to Other Land and Buildings and revalued at £600,000.
findings.matters: Asset values feed into the balance sheet and into any lending or borrowing that relies on asset cover, and the source of the error was the council's own records.
findings.figures: £933,000 overstatement of land and buildings valuations; £360,000 estimated overstatement of investment property; £581,000 reclassified asset; £600,000 revaluation
findings.quote: We assessed the impact of these discrepancies and concluded that they resulted in an overstatement of property valuations of £933,000.

findings.headline: The audit identified six adjustments to the 2025/26 financial statements, with a net £1.3 million effect on the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement and a £0.46 million impact on usable reserves.
findings.detail: The adjustments include a £932,576 reduction in Other Land and Buildings and a £359,908 reduction in Investment Property, both through revaluation losses. The adjustments table records a £46,750 general fund charge for an unaccrued audit fee, which does not match the £0.46 million reserves figure in the summary.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing outturn with audited figures will need the net effect on reserves, and the gap between the summary and the table is one they would check.
findings.figures: £1.3 million net adjustment to CIES; £0.46 million impact on usable reserves; £932,576; £359,908; £46,750 general fund
findings.quote: We have identified six audit adjustments to the financial statements, resulting in a net adjustment of £1.3 million to the Authority's Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement and a £0.46 million impact on usable reserves.

findings.headline: Rother's 2025/26 audit has run from a planned July to September 2026 into October 2026, and the auditor anticipates an unmodified opinion once outstanding matters are resolved.
findings.detail: The revised timetable reflects delays in floor plan documentation, REFCUS accounting, a prior period adjustment, and audit queries when key finance staff were on leave. The audit certificate is also delayed until the NAO completes its Whole of Government Accounts work. Outstanding items are the management representation letter and the final revised accounts for the council and its subsidiary, Rother Housing Company.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, will want to know when Rother's audited 2025/26 accounts are final and whether the opinion is expected to be clean.
findings.figures: Planned completion July to September 2026; extended into October 2026
findings.quote: Our audit was originally planned to be completed between July and September 2026; however, completion has extended into October 2026.

findings.paper_title: Council Tax and Business Rates Collection and Recovery Activity
findings.headline: Government plans to change Council Tax billing and recovery from April 2027, with newly liable taxpayers moving to 12 monthly instalments by default.
findings.detail: The paper says default 12-month billing will extend to all other taxpayers from April 2028, and the period before losing the right to pay by instalments will be extended to at least 63 days. The council says it will prepare operational changes as the detailed requirements are introduced.
findings.matters: Changes to instalment timing and recovery steps alter the cash profile and enforcement timeline for every billing authority, so peers will be planning for the same change.

findings.quote: From April 2027, the Government intends to introduce changes to the statutory Council Tax billing and recovery arrangements.

findings.detail: The paper says the Council 'cannot itself determine or amend' bands or rateable values, so outstanding valuation cases delay billing. Locally, Business Rates valuation cases awaiting action ranged from 5 to 77 between May and October.
findings.matters: Valuation backlogs delay bills and can defer cash receipts, which is a risk to in-year collection for any billing authority.

findings.detail: The paper says these categories 'can restrict or delay the recovery action available to the Council'. They represented 57.3% of accounts and 38.2% of year-end arrears.
findings.matters: A finance director can see how much of the year-end Business Rates debt is blocked by disputes and insolvencies rather than by recovery effort.

findings.paper_title: Council Tax and Business Rates Collection and Recovery Activity
findings.headline: 132 of 702 Business Rates accounts with 2025/26 arrears, worth £238,973.75, have been resolved through payment, relief award or write-off.

findings.headline: The council achieved a balanced 2026/27 budget without drawing on reserves, reversing the trend of the prior two years.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget was approved in balance without reliance on reserves, a material improvement on 2025/26 (£1.4m drawdown) and 2024/25 (£0.69m drawdown). This indicates the council has stabilised underlying spending without further eroding its reserves buffer in the immediate term.
findings.matters: This is the piece of good news: it demonstrates the council can achieve a balanced budget when savings targets are realistic (the 2026/27 savings plan is £0.69m, much smaller than 2025/26's failed £1.1m target, and early tracking shows 85% will be delivered). It also shows the financial stress is not unmanageable in the near term.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget balanced without reserve drawdown; planned savings £0.69m; 85% forecast to be delivered in Q1 2026/27
findings.quote: Consequently, the Council relied more heavily on reserves than anticipated for a second consecutive year, notwithstanding an improved position in 2026/27, where a balanced budget has been approved without the planned use of reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Homelessness costs have tripled in four years and now stand at £3.1m, the council's largest emerging financial pressure.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan identifies homelessness costs at approximately £3.1m, having risen threefold in the prior four years. This represents one of the principal medium-term financial risks and is driving ongoing budget pressure. Demand risk is compounded by the auditor's finding that collection rates for council tax and business rates have declined, reducing forecast income.
findings.matters: A lender funding a council facing rapidly growing demand for statutory services with no control over demand levels (homelessness is driven by external factors) is taking on inflation risk the council cannot contain through savings. Tripling in four years is a structural change, not a temporary fluctuation.
findings.figures: Homelessness costs approximately £3.1m, more than tripled in four years; waste contract costs rising from £5.9m to £7.6m
findings.quote: The MTFP identifies homelessness costs (now around £3.1m, more than tripled in four years)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: General Fund reserves are forecast to decline from £2.5m to £1.2m by 2028/29, cutting the council's buffer by half.
findings.detail: The council's cash reserves are forecast to fall to £1.2m by March 2029 from £2.5m in 2026/27, a decline of £1.3m (52%) over two years. The auditor notes reserves are 'forecast to continue declining' and this represents 'the most significant risks to its medium-term financial resilience'. The council's prior-year recommendation to rebuild reserves remains 'partially addressed'; the council has approved a Reserves Policy but has not yet set a minimum threshold and continues to forecast depletion rather than rebuilding.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's capacity to absorb unexpected costs, shocks or slippage in income or savings delivery. At £1.2m, general reserves represent only 7% of net cost of service—a thin buffer for a council with £10m+ homelessness costs and a £35m contingent loan exposure.
findings.figures: General Reserve falling from £2.5m (2026/27) to £1.2m (2028/29); MTFS & Corporate Development Reserve forecast depleted to zero by 2028/29; forecast fall of £2.1m by March 2028 and further £1.2m by March 2029
findings.quote: General Fund reserves are forecast to continue declining over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for External Auditors Annual Audit Report 2025/26
findings.headline: Council's loan exposure to housing company reached £35.6 million with maturity March 2028 and no homes sold to date.
findings.detail: The Council's loans to Rother DC Housing Company (RDCHC) increased from £9.8m to £33.0m (£35.6m including accrued interest) during the year, funded through external borrowing. Repayment depends on completion and sale of 200 homes; as at 31 March 2026 only three had been completed and none sold. As at July 2026 still no sales had been achieved, though seven are forecast in 2026/27. The loan matures in 28 months. RDCHC losses reached £2.11m in 2025/26, cumulative losses £6.9m. The auditor has raised a new recommendation to strengthen oversight and monitoring of the company's delivery and loan repayment capacity.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liquidity risk. The council borrowed externally to lend to a development company whose ability to repay depends on home sales in a weak housing market. If sales slip further, the council will either have to refinance maturing debt without the expected repayment, or use reserves. With only 28 months to maturity and zero sales recorded to July 2026, this is a live and material exposure.
findings.figures: £35.6m loan exposure (including accrued interest) maturing 31 March 2028; only 3 of 200 planned homes completed; zero sales as at July 2026; RDCHC annual losses £2.11m in 2025/26, cumulative losses £6.9m
findings.quote: The Council's financial exposure to Rother DC Housing Company Ltd (RDCHC) has increased materially to approximately £35.6 million and is funded through external borrowing. The loan agreement has a maturity date of 31 March 2028, with repayment largely dependent on the successful completion and sale of development units. As at 31 March 2026, only three of the planned 200 homes had been completed. Whilst seven open-market sales are forecast during 2026/27 and overall construction completion is expected by September 2027, no homes had been sold as at July 2026.

findings.headline: Council achieved £0.47m of £1.1m savings target (44%) in 2025/26 compared to 87% in 2024/25, primarily due to underperformance in income-generation schemes
findings.detail: The Council achieved only £0.47m of a £1.1m savings target (44%), compared to 87% in 2024/25. The shortfall was concentrated in income-generation schemes dependent on planning fees and commercial income, which were hit by weaker housing market conditions and capacity constraints. The auditor has raised a new recommendation that future savings proposals be underpinned by 'realistic and achievable assumptions' rather than speculative income forecasts.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's ability to balance its budget without drawing reserves would be concerned at the combination of deteriorating savings delivery and continued reliance on reserves. The repeated miss signals either that budget-setting assumptions are too optimistic or that delivery capacity is weak—both risks to financial control.

Critically, the paper notes this evaluation is ongoing and may affect the year-end financial position: 'This may have an impact on the year-end financial position, but it is still being evaluated.'
findings.matters: This creates significant external exposure to a related entity. If the housing company faces repayment difficulties, the council absorbs the loss, and auditor concerns about capacity suggest this is not an academic risk.
findings.figures: Loan provision during 2025/26: £24m; increase to loan provision: £20m; anticipated 2025/26 interest income from RDCHC: £1.870m
findings.quote: It should be noted the External Auditors require the Council to evaluate the loans provided to the RDCHC on an annual basis and consider any anticipated issues with their capacity for repayment under the agreed terms of the loan agreements. This may have an impact on the year-end financial position, but it is still being evaluated.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: Budgeted savings achieved at only 44%, with £611,093 underachievement mainly from planning fee income.
findings.detail: The council set a savings target of £1,084,424 but delivered only £473,328 (44% achievement). £453,584 of savings were rated Red as not deliverable. The largest driver is planning application fee income, which fell £413,000 short of budget. The council attributes this to external economic climate and lack of capacity, factors largely outside management control.
findings.matters: Savings delivery failure suggests either weak financial planning or structural capacity issues. If income-dependent savings miss due to external factors, the council cannot rely on them in future plans.
findings.figures: Target £1,084,424; achieved £473,328; underachievement £611,093; planning fee income deficit £413,000
findings.quote: £453,584 of the savings are rated Red, as they were not deliverable in year. These largely relate to income targets which were unable to be met either due to a lack of capacity or where market forces affected the Council's ability to generate the income anticipated.

findings.paper_title: Budget Outturn 2025/26, Revenue and Capital Monitoring and Flexible Capital Receipts Policy
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve depleted by £1.355m, reducing from £5m to £3.65m in a single year.
findings.detail: The council budgeted for a £694k drawdown but actually drew £1.355m from reserves, a 95% overspend on the planned depletion. This reduces the general reserve by 27%. The paper itself flags this as a risk: continued reductions in reserves could lead to a s114 notice, which is the statutory mechanism for local authority financial failure.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this pace signals financial stress and reduces the council's buffer for unexpected costs or income shocks. A s114 notice would be a significant credit event.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve fell from £5m (1 April 2025) to £3.65m (31 March 2026); actual drawdown £1.355m against budgeted £694k
findings.quote: The Council has a responsibility to operate within a balanced budget and maintain Reserves at an appropriate level. Continued reductions in the Council's reserves would lead to potential risks of a s114 notice.

This medium-priority recommendation has not yet been completed; the paper describes it as 'progressing' as of June 2026. Of eight audit recommendations overall, five are complete and three remain outstanding.

This signals reduced management capacity during a critical organizational change period.

findings.headline: Council has £35m at-risk investment in housing company with repayment dependent on open market sales
findings.detail: Rother has lent £29.15m to its housing company (RDCHC), forecast to rise to £32.3m by March 2026 and peak at £35m in June 2026. Repayment of both principal and capitalised interest depends on open market sales 'subject to market conditions.' The CFO acknowledges 'This represents a risk to the Councils budget and reserves levels, should that risk crystalise.' While there is offsetting monitoring and a pre-sale agreement with a Registered Provider, open market sales risk remains live and material.
findings.matters: This is a large contingent liability. If the housing company's open market sales falter (already subject to economic headwinds given the planning fee decline), the council could face a cliff in cash inflows and be unable to recover the loaned capital or interest.
findings.figures: £29.15m loaned to date; forecast £32.3m by 31 March 2026; £35m peak in June 2026
findings.quote: The level of loans provided to the Councils Housing Company currently stands at £29.15m and is forecast to be £32.3m by 31 March 2026. The investment is forecast to peak in June 2026 at around £35m... The repayment of the loans themselves and the capitalised interest costs due to the Council are predicted on both the income due from the sales to the open market and those to the Registered Provider. The latter is certain, but the former is subject to market conditions. This represents a risk to the Councils budget and reserves levels, should that risk crystalise.

findings.headline: Planning and building control fee income reduced by £120k due to housing downturn
findings.detail: The council has reduced its planning and building control fee income target from £1.46m (2025/26) to £1.34m (2026/27) 'due to the downturn in the housing market and general economic climate.' This demand-led income stream is vulnerable to economic cycles and will continue to be 'monitored regularly to identify any significant adverse variances.'
findings.matters: Demand-led income volatility is a warning sign. The council is already cutting its income forecast and explicitly flags this as a risk area that will need close monitoring.
findings.figures: Reduced from £1.46m to £1.34m (£120k reduction)
findings.quote: We have reduced this target to £1.34m in 2026/27 due to the downturn in the housing market and general economic climate.

findings.headline: Adjustment Support Grant continuation beyond 2026/27 is uncertain; loss would be £447k headwind in 2027/28
findings.detail: The council's funding settlement is now subject to central government confirmation of the Adjustment Support Grant beyond 2026/27. If this grant is not continued, the council's funding picture in 2027/28 will be £447k worse than currently projected, and a further £420k worse in 2028/29. This uncertainty compounds the deficits already forecast.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know what portion of the council's funding is contingent on policy decisions outside its control. The loss of £447k would widen a predicted deficit and force larger reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: £447,000 worse in 2027/28 if Adjustment Support Grant is not continued; £420,000 further impact in 2028/29
findings.quote: If the Adjustment Support Grant is not continued over the term of the MTFP then the funding picture in 2027/8 will be £447,000 worse than reported (& a further £420,000 in 2028/29).

findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation costs have more than tripled in four years and now stand at £3.1m
findings.detail: The council is facing runaway demand-led costs in homelessness and temporary accommodation, now budgeted at approximately £3.1m—more than triple the level of four years ago. The CFO identifies this as a 'significant demand led budget pressure' and acknowledges the activity that drives costs 'remains difficult to predict.' This is the largest demand-led risk on the council's balance sheet.
findings.matters: Homelessness costs are volatile, often statutory, and can force emergency reserve drawdowns. Tripling in four years signals structural demand that is unlikely to reverse and exposes the council to further pressures.
findings.figures: c£3.1m budgeted for 2026/27; more than tripled over four years
findings.quote: The Council is experiencing significant demand led budget pressures, particularly in respect of homelessness and temporary accommodation costs which are now budgeted at c£3.1m and more than have tripled over the last four years.

findings.headline: Pay award negotiations pose £920k unaffordable risk if union claims are met
findings.detail: The council budgeted 3% for staff pay rises, but NJC negotiations opened at least £3,000 or 10% whichever is greater—the CFO explicitly calls these 'unaffordable for the Council and would represent a significant risk to our financial sustainability if agreed.' The additional cost would be approximately £920k above the 3% provision. A multi-year settlement could cost even more (RPI+3% for year 2, RPI+2% for year 3). No agreement has been reached and negotiations may take months.
findings.matters: This is a live, material budget risk that could force the council to draw on reserves mid-year or cut services. It also signals the council has limited headroom for wage pressures.
findings.figures: £920k additional cost if NJC claim is met; 3% was budgeted (c£126k per 1% increase)
findings.quote: Clearly these proposals are unaffordable for the Council and would represent a significant risk to our financial sustainability if agreed. The anticipated additional cost (over the provisional already made in the 2026/27 draft budget for a 3% uplift) would be approximately £920k.

findings.headline: Council has exhausted internal borrowing and is now externally borrowing with £7m more planned
findings.detail: The council has run out of internal cash reserves to fund capital projects and the housing company loan. Over the last 12 months it has become increasingly dependent on external borrowing. It is forecasting a further £7m of external borrowing to support £40m of capital spend over 2026/27–2028/29, though it notes it is 'not currently in a position to materially extend its capital programme if those schemes were not supported by grant funding or available capital receipts.'
findings.matters: A lender needs clarity on the council's cash position and borrowing trajectory. The shift to external borrowing exposes the council to interest rate risk at a time when PWLB rates remain elevated.
findings.figures: £7m of further borrowing forecast for £40m of scheme costs over 2026/27–2028/29
findings.quote: the Council has now exhausted its ability to internally borrowing and over the last 12 months has become increasingly reliant on needing to externally borrow

findings.headline: General reserves forecast to fall from £10.655m (March 2025) to £1.2m (March 2029); council faces £357k deficit 2027/28 and £923k deficit 2028/29
findings.detail: The council has set a balanced budget for 2026/27 but the CFO explicitly warns that the council 'remains on a path whereby reserves will be significantly depleted over the term of the MTFP.' General reserves are forecast to fall from £10.655m (March 2025) to £2.1m (March 2028) to £1.2m (March 2029). The council will have deficits of £357k in 2027/28 and £923k in 2028/29 that will be funded from reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council is burning through financial buffers and will have no reserves left within three years. This is structural insolvency risk.
findings.quote: the Council remains on a path whereby reserves will be significantly depleted over the term of the MTFP

news_drafts.headline: Rother's reserves forecast to halve despite balancing immediate budget
news_drafts.lead: Rother District Council approved a balanced budget for 2026/27 without drawing on reserves, reversing two years in which it had relied on reserves to close budget gaps. However, auditors have flagged that the council's reserves are forecast to decline from £2.5 million in 2026/27 to £1.2 million by March 2029 — a 52 per cent fall. Auditors identify this as the most significant risk to the council's medium-term financial resilience, compounded by a material factor: the council's £35.6 million loan to Rother DC Housing Company, which matures in March 2028. As at July 2026, only three of 200 planned homes had been completed and none sold. The council also achieved only 44 per cent of a £1.1 million savings target in 2025/26, compared with 87 per cent the prior year, due to shortfalls in income-generation schemes.
